scenes.footage: animation: boy under a tree, pan up into the survey's real stars
lines: Have you ever looked up at the night sky, and wondered how many of those stars have planets of their own?
Our galaxy holds hundreds of billions of stars, and most of them likely have at least one planet.
But planets give off no light of their own. From here, they're invisible.

scenes.footage: site: How it works tour, the dip
lines: There is a way to see them. When a planet crosses in front of its star, the star dims, just a little.
NASA's TESS telescope has watched almost the whole sky.
But the dips are faint, most are fakes, and too few people can check them.
So I built Tessa.
She has searched seventy-six thousand stars, and found seven new planet candidates, each with a case file anyone can read.
Here's one, live on my laptop.
Tessa tries over two hundred thousand orbits, and finds a dip every day and a half.
It clears the bar, set by searching the light flipped upside down, where any dip can only be noise.

scenes.footage: localhost /run: code checks, with impostor cards beside it
lines: Most dips aren't planets. They're impostors: two stars eclipsing, starspots, or a neighbour's light.
Code checks for each.
To rank the survivors, I trained an X G Boost model. It scores this one low. On its own, it would have thrown this planet away.
But Tessa doesn't stop there. She investigates.

scenes.footage: localhost /run: Glimmer's tool calls and verdict
lines: The call goes to Muse Glimmer, which I fine-tuned on seven hundred and forty-five investigations written by Muse Spark Open.
Glimmer reads the evidence, decides which measurements it needs, calls those tools itself, and writes a case file with its reasons.
Its verdict: a planet, about three times the size of Earth.
Then TRICERATOPS asks: could anything else make this dip, like one of three hundred nearby stars?
Here, the chance of a false alarm is under one percent.
And I made it ten times faster, without losing any accuracy.

scenes.footage: site: results section (to be redesigned to match)
lines: So how accurate is Tessa?
I tested her on five hundred and seventy-nine past TESS signals with known answers.
When Tessa says planet, she's right ninety-two percent of the time. And she raised fewer than half the false alarms of NASA's ExoMiner plus plus.

scenes.footage: site: Search a star, then Ask Tessa
lines: Anyone can join in at tessa dot brave A I dot solutions.
Search a star in your browser, and ask Tessa's guide, built on Muse Spark, anything.
This is one of her candidates, around a small red star, two hundred and ninety light-years away.
If it's a planet, its star will dim again on the fifth of November.
Now the sky gets to answer.
